title: Personal Issues (Hard Version)
solution: Write p−q = (N mod 2) − zA + zN, where N = n−2 is the number of moves and zA, zN count each player's non-scoring moves. The fight is over who is forced into non-scoring moves, and the value is always 0 or 1. If x and y are adjacent, the zero set is connected, every frontier move scores and no deviation (a c=0 move) helps, so the answer is (n−2) mod 2. Otherwise let x=p_0,...,p_d=y be the path, k=d−1 the number of gap vertices, and h_i the size of the subtree hanging off p_i. The game then reduces to the gap. Everything already reachable behaves like a pile of free scoring moves that matters only by its parity: an odd pile is one spare tempo, i.e. a pass. Taking gap vertex p_i from either end of the gap scores and adds h_i to the pile. The last gap vertex m is the forced merge, flipped with two zero neighbours. Counting parities, Axial wins (answer 1) iff h_m mod 2 equals t = 1 xor (k−1) xor ((h_0+h_d) mod 2) xor (xor over the gap of h_i mod 2). That leaves a game on a bit string: remove a cell from either end, or pass while the pile is odd. In mover-relative terms (c_i=1 if p_i is good for the player to move), a pass exists only on odd-length windows, and it belongs to the player for whom the number of bad cells is even. Solving this with an O(k^2) interval win/lose DP is the easy version. With k up to 2·10^5 that is too slow. Instead, on an odd window the result depends only on the middle cell and the mirrored-pair sums s_j = c_{m−j}+c_{m+j}, read outward from the center by a 3-state automaton. With a good middle: state A moves to B on s=0 and wins on anything else. State B loses on s=1, returns to A on s=2, and moves to C on s=0. State C loses on s=1 and stays otherwise. Running out of pairs wins. A bad middle is the complement. On an even window the mover removes one end, so the mover wins iff either odd sub-window loses for the opponent. Finding the path and the hanging sizes is a BFS/DFS, so the whole solution is O(n). The reductions (pile parity, merge-vertex criterion, pass ownership, automaton) were found and validated by exhaustive search rather than proved.

solution_check.how: sol.py (O(n): BFS path, hanging-size flood, parity target, center-out 3-state scan) prints 1 1 0 0 on the 4-case sample, matching. brute.cpp is an exhaustive minimax over all 2^n zero-sets. It agreed with sol.py on 6000 random trees with n in 2..18 (30 seeds x 200; shapes were uniform random, bounded-depth, long-spine and spine+bushy, with x,y random or at the spine ends) and on 450 trees with n in 18..22. The intermediate reductions were checked separately. The connected-zero-set value equals r mod 2 on 3000 random trees (Python brute). Outside regions matter only by parity on 4000 constructed trees. The path game (interval DP model) matched brute on 4000 trees with n<=13 and on 800+ trees with n 10..22. The 3-state scan matched the O(k^2) interval game DP on 20000 random bit strings of length 1..45. The automaton came from Myhill-Nerode learning (8 classes, closed under transitions). sol.py matched the O(d^2) model on 500 trees with n 50..400. An n=2·10^5 input with a 1.5·10^5-vertex path runs in about 0.1 s.

rejected_tags.reason: The only traversal is one BFS/flood that finds the x-y path and counts the vertices hanging off each path vertex. That is scaffolding, and sol.py itself uses BFS. This also matches the H1 review, which dropped the same tag for the same reason. The judge's 'trees' tag is kept as 'tree'.

notes.solver: game-theory (0.95): two-player optimal-play game. The whole solution is a win/lose analysis: who is forced into non-scoring moves, tempo/pass ownership, and which path vertex survives as the merge. parity-argument (0.8): this is what makes the problem tractable. Only parities matter: the parity of the remaining count in the connected phase, outside regions only by size parity (an odd pile = one pass), the parity of the merge vertex's hanging subtree deciding the winner, and pass ownership by the parity of bad cells in an odd window. Considered and rejected: game-dp and interval-dp. The O(d^2) interval win/lose DP over (left,right,pile parity) solves only the easy version (H1, n<=3000); here d can be 2·10^5, so the hard version needs the center-out characterization instead. Those labels belong on H1, not H2. Also rejected: dfs/bfs as patterns (only scaffolding to extract the x–y path and hanging subtree sizes; kept dfs as a tag), palindrome (the scan compares mirrored pairs but is not about palindromes), greedy (no greedy rule, the play is minimax), subtree-dp/tree-dp (hanging sizes are a plain flood, no DP on the tree), constructive-algorithm and simulation.
notes.skeptic:
SOLUTION: correct, as far as exhaustive and stress testing can show. The proposal says plainly that it is unproved, and I did not prove it either. My derivation came first. With an exact minimax brute force I found that the answer depends only on d=dist(x,y), on (h_0+h_d) mod 2 and on h_1..h_{d-1} mod 2, and that it is always 0 or 1. This agrees with the H1 framing: the game is normal play on scoring moves, the last path vertex m is never scored, and Axial wins iff n-3-h_m is odd (equivalently h_m mod 2 == t). A merge with c=3, set up by a c=0 move into the merge vertex's hanging subtree, explains why h_m's parity matters (sample 4 and my d=2 hand case). The proposal's O(n) scan agrees with the brute force on every free tree up to n=14 with every {x,y}, on every caterpillar parity pattern up to d=12, and on adversarial trees up to n=25. I rebuilt the abstract window game myself from the text. It matches the brute force, and the 3-state centre-out automaton matches it up to d=1000. The automaton's centre-out direction comes from the mirror strategy in take-from-either-end games: answering every end removal with the opposite end keeps the window centred. Passes (an odd free-move pile) are what need the extra automaton states.

PATTERNS. game-theory: keep (0.95). It is a two-player optimal-play game, and the whole solution is win/lose analysis: tempo, passes, who is forced into the merge, and the mirror-strategy structure. parity-argument: keep (0.85). It is the load-bearing step, not decoration. Hanging subtrees count only mod 2, the free-move pile is one pass when it is odd, x's and y's hangers combine by XOR, and the survivor's parity decides the winner.

NEAR-MISS TRAP (the brief's bitmask-dp vs interval-dp analogue): interval-dp and game-dp are correctly absent. The O(k^2) interval DP over [l,r] plus a pile bit is the H1 solution (n<=3000, which permits the O(n^2) table). H2 has the same statement with n<=2e5, and the constraint is exactly what rules that DP out. H2 needs the linear centre-out characterisation. So H1 = game-dp + interval-dp and H2 = no DP label. That difference is the pair's distinguishing signal and should be kept. I considered adding game-dp because the automaton is a finite-state compression of the window DP. I rejected it: off-centre windows are reachable, so no natural O(n) DP over nested centred windows exists without the learned 3-state characterisation, and what is distinctive is the characterisation, not a DP. bitmask-dp: the 2^n minimax is only a verifier.

TRAP binary-search-answer: does not apply and was not proposed. The output is 0/1 from a win/lose game. There is no monotone parameter and no feasibility test.

TREE-SPECIFIC LABELS (asked by the caller): the tree work is root at x (or BFS), extract the x-y path and take each path vertex's hanging size (sz(p_i) - sz(p_{i+1}) - 1 when rooted at x, or a flood that avoids the path). Only the parity of those counts is used. No DP state is indexed by a subtree and nothing is combined over children, so subtree-dp/tree-dp would send a 'tree dp' searcher to a path parity game. Rejected, consistent with the H1 review. dfs/bfs are scaffolding (rejected as patterns, and the dfs tag is dropped). tree-center is a false friend: the scan starts at the midpoint of the x-y path, not at the tree's centre (the eccentricity minimiser). tree-diameter is not used. The judge's 'trees' tag stays as the tag 'tree'. Also rejected: palindrome (the scan sums mirrored pairs but is not about palindromes), greedy (play is minimax), grundy-numbers (a single win/lose game, and pile-as-pass is covered by parity-argument), constructive-algorithm, simulation, brute-force (verifier only).

TAGS: dfs dropped (see rejected_tags). game-theory, tree and math kept; math is for the proof-style parity reasoning.

SUMMARY: the proposal's 65-word version was accurate. I rewrote it to (a) say the value is always 0 or 1 and that it is decided by which x-y path vertex survives, which is the non-obvious reduction, (b) change 'neighbour' to 'neighbor' to match the statement and the H1 summary for lexical search, and (c) keep n ≤ 2·10^5 and the centre-out linear scan. I kept the words 'interval DP' out of it on purpose, so H2 does not match interval-dp queries meant for H1. 69 words.
